prompts.prompt_text:
I'm working on a set of service-outage reports about supposed violations to the Business SLA shared between the company and it's business clients. I need you to go through one to determine whether or not it is describing a scenario with a valid stop-clock-condition from amongst our company's list of valid stop-clock-conditions. If there are, then I need you to write an email to be sent to our record keeping department that addresses what service problem(s) occurred, why they occurred, which condition(s) have been met, and that this means the outage period must be excluded from the official downtime calculations. Make sure to include the total time that should be excluded. If there is a condition that looks like it might be valid at first but isn't due to any reason, you still need to include it in the email but it should be explicitly stated as an invalid reason and why. This is because it will be scrutinized by their workers and including such "false positive" conditions in the email rapidly speeds up their own review process. Here is the list of stop-clock-conditions:

1 END-USER REQUEST
Periods when a restoration or testing effort is delayed at the specific
request of the End-User. The SCC shall exist during the period the
Contractor was delayed, provided that the End-User’s request is
documented and time stamped in the Contractor’s trouble ticket or Service
Request system and shows efforts are made to contact the End-User
during the applicable Stop Clock period.
2 OBSERVATION
Time after a service has been restored but End-User request ticket is kept
open for observation. If the service is later determined by the End-User to
not have been restored, the Stop Clock shall continue until the time the
End-User notifies the Contractor that the Service has not been restored.
3 END-USER NOT AVAILABLE
Time after a service has been restored but End-User is not available to
verify that the Service is working. If the service is later determined by the
End-User to not have been restored, the Stop Clock shall apply only for the
time period between Contractor’s reasonable attempt to notify the End-
User that Contractor believes the service has been restored and the time
the End-User notifies the Contractor that the Service has not been
restored.
4 WIRING
Restoration cannot be achieved because the problem has been isolated to
wiring that is not maintained by Contractor or any of its Subcontractors or
Affiliates. If it is later determined the wiring is not the cause of failure, the
SCC shall not apply.
5 POWER Trouble caused by a power problem outside of the responsibility of the
Contractor.
6 CUSTOMER
PROVISIONING DELAY
Delays to Provisioning caused by lack of Customer’s building entrance
Facilities, conduit structures that are the Customer’s responsibilities or
Extended demarcation wiring. If the Service Providing Contractor has been
contracted by the Customer for extended demarcation, this SCC shall not
apply to missed dates/times. The Customer Provisioning Delay SCC is
restricted to Provisioning SLAs only.
7 ACCESS
Limited access or contact with End-User provided the Contractor
documents in the trouble ticket several efforts to contact End-User for the
following:
a. Access necessary to correct the problem is not available because
access has not been arranged by site contact or End-User
representative;
b. Site contact refuses access to technician who displays proper
identification;
c. Customer provides incorrect site contact information which prevents
access, provided that Contractor takes reasonable steps to notify End-
User of the improper contact information and takes steps to obtain the
correct information; or,
d. Site has limited hours of business that directly impacts the
Contractor’s ability to resolve the problem.
If it is determined later that the cause of the problem was not at the site in
question, then the Access SCC shall not apply.
8 STAFF
Any problem or delay to the extent caused by End-User’s staff that prevents
or delays Contractor’s resolution of the problem.
In such event, Contractor shall make a timely request to End-User staff to
correct the problem or delay and document in trouble ticket.
9 APPLICATION End-User software applications that interfere with repair of the trouble.
10 CPE
Repair/replacement of Customer Premise Equipment (CPE) not provided
by Contractor if the problem has been isolated to the CPE. If determined
later that the CPE was not the cause of the service outage, the CPE SCC
will not apply.
11 NO RESPONSE
Failure of the trouble ticket originator or responsible End-User to return a
call from Contractor’s technician for on-line close of trouble tickets after the
Service has been restored as long as Contractor can provide
documentation in the trouble ticket substantiating the communication from
Contractor’s technician.
12
MAINTENANCE
An outage directly related to any properly performed scheduled
maintenance or upgrade scheduled for CALNET DNCS service. Any such
stop clock condition shall not extend beyond the scheduled period of the
maintenance or upgrade. SLAs shall apply for any maintenance caused
outage beyond the scheduled maintenance period. Outages occurring
during a scheduled maintenance or upgrade period and not caused by the
scheduled maintenance shall not be subject to the Maintenance SCC.
13
THIRD PARTY
Any problem or delay caused by a third party not under the control of
Contractor, not preventable by Contractor, including, at a minimum, cable
cuts not caused by the Contractor. Contractor’s Subcontractors and
Affiliates shall be deemed to be under the control of Contractor with respect
to the equipment, services, or Facilities to be provided under this Contract.
14 FORCE MAJEURE
Force Majeure events, as defined in the eVAQ General Provisions -
Telecommunications, Section 28 (Force Majeure).
15
CUSTOMER
ENVIRONMENTAL
An outage directly caused by customer premise environmental conditions,
which are outside the control and responsibility of the Contractor. This
includes a non-secured location, excessive heat or lack of cooling. If
determined later that the environmental conditions were not the cause of
the service outage, or a result of the Contractor modifying Contractor
provided equipment without Customer’s approval, the Customer
Environmental SCC will not apply.

**Subject:** Stop-Clock Validation Request: OmnomnomCorp Outage (Ticket #INC-9942)

**To:** Record Keeping Department
**From:** Service Outage Reporting Team
**Date:** October 26, 2023

**Re:** Service Outage Report – OmnomnomCorp (Ticket #INC-9942)

Dear Record Keeping Team,

Please review the attached service-outage report for OmnomnomCorp (Ticket #INC-9942). This report details a significant service interruption that requires the exclusion of specific time periods from the official downtime calculations due to valid Stop-Clock Conditions (SCCs).

**Service Problem Summary**
The service outage began at 08:00 AM with a Loss of Signal (LOS) alarm at the SmartJack. Upon investigation, the initial diagnosis isolated the fault to internal wiring at the client's demarcation point. However, further testing at 01:00 PM revealed that the internal wiring was actually functional. The root cause was identified as a blown fuse inside the Service Provider's SmartJack (Contractor equipment), likely caused by a power surge. Service was fully restored at 01:15 PM, and the ticket was closed at 02:30 PM.

**Validated Stop-Clock Conditions**
The following conditions have been verified as valid based on the troubleshooting timeline:

1.  **Condition 7: ACCESS**
    *   **Time Period:** 09:30 AM – 10:45 AM (1 Hour 15 Minutes)
    *   **Justification:** The Contractor arrived on-site but was denied access to the server room by security until 10:45 AM. The Contractor documented multiple attempts to contact the Site Contact (Mr. Smith) to arrange access, and the Site Contact eventually arrived to verify credentials. This meets the criteria for limited access delayed by End-User arrangements.
2.  **Condition 1: END-USER REQUEST**
    *   **Time Period:** 11:45 AM – 01:00 PM (1 Hour 15 Minutes)
    *   **Justification:** The Site Contact (Mr. Smith) explicitly requested that all testing and technician activity cease until 1:00 PM due to a shareholder meeting. The Contractor documented this request in the trouble ticket and waited on-site as directed.
3.  **Condition 11: NO RESPONSE**
    *   **Time Period:** 01:20 PM – 02:30 PM (1 Hour 10 Minutes)
    *   **Justification:** Service was restored at 01:15 PM. The Contractor attempted to contact the trouble ticket originator (Mr. Smith) at 01:20 PM to verify the restoration, but received no response. The ticket was not closed until 02:30 PM when Mr. Smith returned the call to confirm service. This meets the criteria for failure to return a call after restoration.

**Total Time to Exclude from Official Downtime:**
**3 Hours 40 Minutes**

**Invalid/False Positive Conditions**
The following conditions were initially considered but do not apply to this specific scenario. These are included for your scrutiny to prevent future false positives:

1.  **Condition 4: WIRING**
    *   **Status:** **Invalid**
    *   **Reason:** While the contractor initially isolated the problem to internal wiring at the demarcation point (11:30 AM), it was later determined at 01:00 PM that the wiring was functional and the actual issue was a blown fuse in the SmartJack. Per Condition 4, if wiring is determined not to be the cause of failure, the SCC shall not apply.
2.  **Condition 10: CPE**
    *   **Status:** **Invalid**
    *   **Reason:** The report identifies the issue as a blown fuse inside the "Service Provider's SmartJack (Contractor equipment)." Condition 10 applies only to Customer Premise Equipment (CPE) *not* provided by the Contractor.
3.  **Condition 3: END-USER NOT AVAILABLE**
    *   **Status:** **Invalid**
    *   **Reason:** While the Service was restored and the End-User was not immediately available to verify, Condition 11 (No Response) is the specific provision for scenarios where the Contractor attempts to close the ticket via call and the End-User fails to return it. Condition 3 is typically reserved for physical unavailability preventing verification while the Contractor is on-site waiting. Given that the Contractor made a specific call attempt (Condition 11) rather than waiting in silence, Condition 11 is the accurate classification. Including Condition 3 here would be redundant and inaccurate.

**Conclusion**
Based on the evidence provided in the trouble ticket, we request that the total of **3 Hours 40 Minutes** be excluded from the official downtime calculations for this incident.

Please let us know if you require further documentation or clarification regarding these stop-clock validations.

Best regards,

Service Outage Reporting Team

Upon inspection, the initial hypothesis suggested internal wiring or power issues; however, the final root cause was identified as a blown fuse inside the Contractor-provided SmartJack, which was replaced at 01:15 PM, restoring service.

**Valid Stop-Clock Conditions (SCC)**
The following conditions have been met and are valid for exclusion from official downtime calculations:

1.  **SCC 7 (ACCESS):**
    *   **Details:** Field technicians arrived at the facility at 09:30 AM but were unable to enter the server room. The security desk was unmanned, and the security guard refused access until the Site Contact (Mr. Smith) arrived to clear the technician.
    *   **Excluded Period:** 09:30 AM to 10:45 AM.
    *   **Duration:** 1 Hour 15 Minutes.

2.  **SCC 1 (END-USER REQUEST):**
    *   **Details:** At 11:45 AM, the Site Contact requested the technician halt all testing and activity immediately due to a shareholder meeting in the adjacent conference room. The technician documented this request in the ticketing system at 11:50 AM and waited in the vehicle until the meeting concluded.
    *   **Excluded Period:** 11:45 AM to 01:00 PM.
    *   **Duration:** 1 Hour 15 Minutes.

**Invalid Stop-Clock Conditions (False Positives)**
The following conditions were evaluated but are deemed invalid for the reasons listed. These are included to facilitate your review process:

1.  **SCC 4 (WIRING):**
    *   **Reason for Invalidity:** While the technician initially updated the ticket at 11:30 AM stating the problem was "isolated to internal extended wiring," subsequent testing revealed the issue was a blown fuse within the Contractor's SmartJack equipment. Per the SCC definition, this condition does not apply if it is later determined the wiring is not the cause of failure.
2.  **SCC 5 (POWER):**
    *   **Reason for Invalidity:** The technician encountered a dead PDU outlet (11:10 AM), which appeared to be a customer power issue. However, the outage was ultimately resolved by replacing the SmartJack fuse (Contractor equipment). Therefore, the power problem was not the root cause of the service outage.
3.  **SCC 3 (END-USER NOT AVAILABLE):**
    *   **Reason for Invalidity:** Service was restored at 01:15 PM. While the primary contact (Mr. Smith) was unavailable, the Secondary Contact (Ms. Jones) was reached at 01:30 PM and confirmed the service was working. As the End-User was available to verify the restoration through an authorized representative, the Stop Clock ceased at 01:30 PM.
4.  **SCC 11 (NO RESPONSE):**
    *   **Reason for Invalidity:** Similar to SCC 3, while the primary contact did not return the call immediately after restoration, the Secondary Contact responded to the technician's call and confirmed the service status. This satisfies the requirement for communication from the End-User.

**Total Excluded Time**
Based on the valid conditions identified above (SCC 7 and SCC 1), the total outage period to be excluded from official downtime calculations is **2 Hours and 30 Minutes**.

Please update the official SLA records to reflect this exclusion.

Regards,

Service Management Team

**To:** Record Keeping Department
**From:** Service Delivery Management
**Date:** October 26, 2023
**Re:** Stop-Clock Condition Validation for Ticket #INC-9942

Dear Record Keeping Team,

Please find below the analysis of the service outage report for Ticket #INC-9942 regarding OmnomnomCorp. We have reviewed the timeline against the Business SLA Stop-Clock Conditions (SCC).

**Service Problem & Root Cause**
*   **Problem:** Loss of Signal (LOS) at SmartJack resulting in service hard down.
*   **Root Cause:** A blown fuse inside the Service Provider's SmartJack (Contractor equipment), likely caused by a power surge.
*   **Resolution:** Fuse replacement and SmartJack reset performed by Field Tech.

**Valid Stop-Clock Conditions**
The following conditions have been met and documented in the trouble ticket system. The associated time periods must be excluded from the official SLA calculations.

1.  **SCC 7 – ACCESS (09:30 AM – 10:45 AM)**
    *   **Reason:** Field Tech was denied access by site security due to ID badge protocol discrepancies despite displaying valid company ID and Work Order. Site Contact was initially unavailable to verify access.
    *   **Validation:** Multiple contact attempts documented (09:30, 09:45). Access granted at 10:45 AM. The problem was located at the site (SmartJack), satisfying the requirement that the cause be at the site in question.
    *   **Duration:** 1 Hour 15 Minutes.

2.  **SCC 1 – END-USER REQUEST (11:45 AM – 01:00 PM)**
    *   **Reason:** End-User (Mr. Smith) explicitly requested all testing and technician activity cease due to a shareholder meeting until 1:00 PM.
    *   **Validation:** Request was documented and time-stamped in the ticket at 11:50 AM. Tech made a reasonable effort to contact the End-User during the wait period (12:30 PM call attempt).
    *   **Duration:** 1 Hour 15 Minutes.

3.  **SCC 11 – NO RESPONSE (01:20 PM – 02:30 PM)**
    *   **Reason:** Failure of the ticket originator (Mr. Smith) to return calls for ticket closure after service restoration.
    *   **Validation:** Service was restored at 01:15 PM. Tech attempted to verify/close with Mr. Smith at 01:20 PM (Voicemail). Mr. Smith returned the call at 02:30 PM to confirm service and close the ticket.
    *   **Duration:** 1 Hour 10 Minutes.
    *   *Note:* This exclusion applies to the **Resolution SLA** clock, as service was restored at 01:15 PM. SCC 1 and SCC 7 apply to the **Availability/Downtime SLA** clock.

**Invalid Stop-Clock Conditions (False Positives)**
The following conditions appeared applicable during initial troubleshooting but were determined invalid upon final root cause analysis. These are included for audit transparency.

1.  **SCC 4 – WIRING (Invalid)**
    *   **Initial Indication:** At 11:30 AM, the Tech updated the ticket stating the problem was isolated to "internal extended wiring."
    *   **Reason for Invalidity:** At 01:15 PM, further inspection revealed the root cause was a blown fuse within the Contractor's SmartJack, not the wiring. Per SCC 4 guidelines: "If it is later determined the wiring is not the cause of failure, the SCC shall not apply."

2.  **SCC 5 – POWER (Invalid)**
    *   **Initial Indication:** At 11:00 AM, the SmartJack showed no power, and the Client PDU outlet appeared dead.
    *   **Reason for Invalidity:** The power loss was due to an internal fuse failure within the Contractor's SmartJack, not an external power failure outside Contractor responsibility. Therefore, this does not meet the criteria for a Power SCC exclusion.

**Total Time Excluded from SLA Calculations**
*   **Total Stop-Clock Time:** 3 Hours 40 Minutes
    *   (01h 15m Access + 01h 15m End-User Request + 01h 10m No Response)

Please adjust the official downtime and resolution records for OmnomnomCorp accordingly to reflect these exclusions. Let me know if you require the specific ticket logs to substantiate these timestamps.

Best regards,

Service Delivery Management

I need help figuring out the schedule for the bar/restaurant this weekend (Th-Su). I have a lot of requests for time off.

Friday: Barback-Leo; Bar Open 3pm-Joe; Bar 6pm-Carrie; Bar 8pm-Sarah; Bar 8pm-Ken; Serve Open 3pm-Nat; Serve Open 3pm-Mary; Serve 6pm-Kelly; Serve 6pm-Ray

Saturday: Barback-Brett; Bar Open 3pm-Sarah; Bar 6pm-Joe; Bar 8pm-Carrie; Bar 8pm-Ken; Serve Open 3pm-Nat; Serve Open 3pm-Pablo; Serve 6pm-Kelly; Serve 6pm-Mary

Sunday: Bar Open 3pm-Ray; Serve Open 3pm-Pablo

-------

Ray, Pablo, and Brett are all going to be out of town all weekend.

Nat and Kelly have plans on Thursday.

Mary has plans on Sunday.

-------

Give people who are normally on the schedule priority over temp fill-ins, but we can't have anyone working four days in a row.

Erin, Tom, and Sally can possibly fill in for server shifts that can't be covered, but I would prefer not to use Tom as it didn't go well last time I called him in. If all else fails, I can fill in an empty shifts myself. Sally has her other serving job on Sat/Sun.

Let me know the final schedule for this weekend (Th-Su), and please bold shifts that cannot be filled in by people normally on the schedule. If multiple people could possibly fill the shift, put both of their names there with a slash in between them and I'll figure it out from there. Do not put me on the schedule - just leave a question mark in bold if there is really no one according to the provided information that can fill in the shift, including temps. Obviously I'll have to ask temps first, but just write their names in for now if they are the only option.

Also, don't fill in both shifts for the 6pm serve shift on Thursday if that is possible, we can do it with just two servers for that day.

prompts.prompt_text:
Right ok so I’m ta’ing for a class and we need to do some grade calculations and analysis. There are 30 students, 7 assignments each, all of them out of 25 points. So the category of assignments these are in will add up to 175 points but i also need the percentage for each student. And i want a per student breakdown but then also one that looks at each assignment for the class as a whole.
So first would be the per student breakdown so give me a list of all the students. I need their point total out of 175 first, then their percentage, then their letter grade based on this scale:
A+ = 97–100%
A = 93–96%
A− = 90–92%
B+ = 87–89%
B = 83–86%
B− = 80–82%
C+ = 77–79%
C = 73–76%
C− = 70–72%
D+ = 67–69%
D = 63–66%
D− = 60–62%
F = 0–59%
Then after that i need to know each student’s best assignment and worst assignment, and if they have multiple best/worst assignments, you can list them all. So like if someone scores 25 on assignments 4 and 7, you can list assignments 4 and 7 for their best assignments. List best first then worst.
Oh and make the student list alphabetical by last initial, write the point total in bold and like “167/175,” bold the percentage, and bold the letter grade. Put the letter grade in parentheses next to the percentage. don’t list them using bullets/numbers. And the student names should be bolded and capitalized.

So then for the second part, i want a breakdown by assignment, so for each assignment i need some stats. Tell me the average score of the assignment, in points and then in percentage with the letter grade in parentheses next to the percentage. If any students get a perfect score, list their names next, and same for if any students get a zero. Put the assignment name (e.g., “assignment #4”) in bold.

Oh and for the first part, the student breakdown, underneath everything you already listed, if any student has a 0 on an assignment, put a note saying so and specifying the assignment, like this: “*0 on assignment #_” so the prof knows to talk to them. If any student has a grade of C or below, also list a note that says “*low grade, professor to meet with student”

And then at the end of the second part, tell me which assignment has the best average score and which has the worst.

Below are my notes about Homeostatic Regulation for my Health and Disease class. Can you please help me make flashcards to study the material for an upcoming test? I need to know everything, so please don’t omit any details. Also, please don’t present the information in bullet points since it will be easier to copy and paste them into my quiz program without them. For words or phrases that have an explicit definition (usually preceded by a colon), please just use the word or phrase as the question. For example – “Homeostasis” is the question and “the integrative action of the systems of an organism that result in the maintenance of the optimal internal environment despite variations in the external conditions” is the answer. For examples of feedback systems, you can just put the entire thing on one card since they’re all tied together. Other than examples (including the feedback system examples and dashes that start with “ex:”) or lists (like the levels of organization of the body), please put every dash or bullet point on a separate flashcard. For information that is presented in standalone sentences, please word the question as a natural question. For example – “Homeostasis is controlled through negative feedback” could use the question of “How is homeostasis controlled?” and the answer of “Homeostasis is controlled through negative feedback”. Sometimes you might have to incorporate the header into the question in order for it to make sense on its own, like “properties of produced messages” would need to be mentioned with “nervous system” in order for me to understand that the question is about properties of messages produced by the nervous system. Please bold the question and leave the answers in regular font.  
HOMEOSTATIC REGULATION
Levels of the organization of the body: 
•	Chemical or molecular levels
•	Cellular level
•	Tissue level
•	Organ level 
There are eleven organ systems in the human body, and intercommunication exists between them all.
Homeostasis: the integrative action of the systems of an organism that result in the maintenance of the optimal internal environment despite variations in the external conditions
•	Homeostatic regulation is the adjustment of physiological systems to preserve homeostasis
•	Homeostasis is controlled through negative feedback
Blood levels of glucose is an example of homeostatic regulation.
•	Any time there is a meal there is a peak in blood sugar.
•	Any carbohydrates that are consumed are broken down, solubilized, and enter the blood. We can measure this concentration change.
•	Disease can be monitored using this trend. People who have a challenge in glucose metabolism (diabetics) have larger peaks.
Mechanisms of homeostatic regulation:
1.	Autoregulation: intrinsic regulation
•	Activities of cell, tissue, organ, organ system change when faced with environmental variation
•	Ex: oxygen to cells
2.	Extrinsic regulation
•	Via the nervous and endocrine system
•	Control activities of many organ systems
•	Ex: exercise and oxygen use
A receptor, control center, and an effector are needed for homeostatic regulation.
•	Receptor: a sensor that is sensitive to a particular variable or stimulus
•	Control center: integration center, receives and processes information supplied by the receptor
•	Effector: a cell or organ that responds to the commands of the control center and whose activity opposes (negative feedback) or enhances (positive feedback) the stimulus
Body temperature regulation: example of a negative feedback system
•	Homeostasis: normal body temperature (37 degrees)
•	Stimulus: body temperature rises, normal temperature disturbed
•	Receptors: temperature sensors in skin and hypothalamus
•	Control center: thermoregulatory center in brain
•	Effectors: receives signal from the brain to cause sweat glands in skin to increase secretion and blood vessels in skin to dilate
•	Response: increased heat loss, body temperature drops, normal temperature restored
•	Internal fluctuations are smaller than environmental fluctuations (36.7-37.2)
Positive feedback
•	Rarely encountered
•	Tends to produce extreme results
•	Initial stimulus produces a response that exaggerates or enhances effects
•	Positive feedback loops are encountered when a potentially dangerous or stressful process must be completed quickly before homeostasis can be restored
Blood clotting response: example of a positive feedback system
•	Break in blood vessel wall causes bleeding
•	Damaged cells release chemicals
•	Clotting begins
•	Additional chemicals released, clotting accelerates
•	Blood clot plugs break in vessel wall; bleeding stops
•	The clotting response encourages the occurrence of more clotting.
•	When blood loss occurs, blood pressure and heart rate lowers because the body responds first to stop the bleeding and then it restores blood pressure.
Clotters: the nervous and endocrine system
•	The nervous and endocrine systems are the major homeostatic control systems of the body
•	Neuron
-	Stimulus induces (1) permeability increase, (2) Na+ and Ca2+ influx, (3) depolarization 
-	Secretion follows (1) depolarization, (2) permeability increase, (3) Ca2+ influx
-	Neurons that pass signals between each other are physically close
•	Simple endocrine cell: releases a signal into the blood, as generally mediated by calcium, and the signal can often travel farther and last longer.
Properties of produced messages
•	Nervous system: very private, very fast transmission (ms), very short message length (ms)
•	Endocrine system: less private, slow transmission (s), long message length (s, min, hr, days, weeks, etc)
Homeostasis at the cellular level is maintained through the action of cell membranes that maintain cell integrity, control cell activities, and have electrical activity that lead cell to cell signalling.
A fluid membrane surrounds our cells.
•	Membrane composition can vary
•	Integral proteins: serve as passive transport pores and channels, active-transport pumps and carriers, membrane-linked enzymes, and chemical signal receptors
•	Peripheral proteins: membrane-linked, do not extend through the membrane
•	Glycoproteins: have oligosaccharide side chains that are vital for cell recognition, interactions, adhesion, and communication
Intracellular signals are coordinated.

**How many organ systems are in the human body and what exists between them?**
There are eleven organ systems in the human body, and intercommunication exists between them all.

**Homeostasis**
the integrative action of the systems of an organism that result in the maintenance of the optimal internal environment despite variations in the external conditions

**What is homeostatic regulation?**
Homeostatic regulation is the adjustment of physiological systems to preserve homeostasis

**How is homeostasis controlled?**
Homeostasis is controlled through negative feedback

**How are blood levels of glucose an example of homeostatic regulation?**
Any time there is a meal there is a peak in blood sugar. Any carbohydrates that are consumed are broken down, solubilized, and enter the blood. We can measure this concentration change. Disease can be monitored using this trend. People who have a challenge in glucose metabolism (diabetics) have larger peaks.

**Autoregulation**
intrinsic regulation

**What occurs during autoregulation?**
Activities of cell, tissue, organ, organ system change when faced with environmental variation. Ex: oxygen to cells.

**What is extrinsic regulation?**
Via the nervous and endocrine system. Control activities of many organ systems. Ex: exercise and oxygen use.

**What components are needed for homeostatic regulation?**
A receptor, control center, and an effector are needed for homeostatic regulation.

**Receptor**
a sensor that is sensitive to a particular variable or stimulus

**Control center**
integration center, receives and processes information supplied by the receptor

**Effector**
a cell or organ that responds to the commands of the control center and whose activity opposes (negative feedback) or enhances (positive feedback) the stimulus

Response: increased heat loss, body temperature drops, normal temperature restored. Internal fluctuations are smaller than environmental fluctuations (36.7-37.2).

Rarely encountered.

Tends to produce extreme results.

Initial stimulus produces a response that exaggerates or enhances effects.

**When are positive feedback loops encountered?**
Positive feedback loops are encountered when a potentially dangerous or stressful process must be completed quickly before homeostasis can be restored.

Break in blood vessel wall causes bleeding. Damaged cells release chemicals. Clotting begins. Additional chemicals released, clotting accelerates. **1. Math Strategy**
*   **Calculator:** The GED math test allows a specific calculator (TI-30XS). Practice using it thoroughly. Know how to use the square root, fractions, and memory functions.

*   **Units:** Always check the units in the question (inches vs. feet, cm vs. m).
*   **Time Management:** Do not get stuck on one question. Mark it and move on.

**2. Science Strategy**
*   **Passage First:** Read the question first, then read the passage. This helps you know what information to look for.
*   **Graphs:** Learn to interpret graphs and charts quickly. Look at the labels on the X and Y axes.
*   **Vocabulary:** Know the difference between independent and dependent variables.

**3. Time Management**
*   **Pomodoro Technique:** If you feel overwhelmed, study for 25 minutes and take a 5-minute break.
*   **Sleep:** Do not sacrifice sleep for studying. Your brain needs sleep to retain the information you are learning. Stick to the 8-hour goal.
*   **Hydration:** Drink water while studying. Dehydration causes brain fog.

*   **Read Carefully:** GED questions often include words like "NOT," "EXCEPT," or "LEAST." Circle these words.
*   **Eliminate Answers:** If you don't know the answer, eliminate the obviously wrong ones first to increase your odds of guessing correctly.
*   **Review:** If you have time left at the end of the test, review your answers, but only change them if you are sure you made a mistake.

I received this feedback from the client on the landing page copy we just sent for approval:

General Thoughts:

Make sure to use "Niagara-on-the-Lake" consistently throughout the copy, not just "Niagara." It’s important and needs to be accurate everywhere.

The wording could use a little more urgency. “Book now” works, but maybe something like “Limited time offer!” or “Hurry, spots are filling up fast!” would make it feel a bit more exclusive.

Icewine Time Copy:

"There’s no time like Icewine time in Niagara!" – This comes off as too cheesy. A more straightforward approach would be better, like: “January is the best time to experience Icewine in Niagara-on-the-Lake.”

"Let us pamper you..." feels a bit too casual. Maybe try something like: “Indulge in a luxurious winter getaway” or “Experience a true winter retreat.” It would sound a bit more refined.

The Icewine martini feels a little forced. It doesn’t really capture the essence of what people come to Niagara for. A focus on the actual Icewine would be better. For example: “Enjoy locally crafted Icewine paired with a delicious charcuterie plate” would feel more in line with the experience.

Christmas Wonderland Garden Copy:

"This holiday discover the Christmas Wonderland Garden in Niagara!" – Don’t forget it should be Niagara-on-the-Lake. That’s important to get right.

The description of the garden sounds great, but it could use a little more magic. For instance, instead of “transformed The Gardens at Pillar and Post,” you might say, “Transformed The Gardens at Pillar and Post into a sparkling holiday wonderland.” This feels a little more festive and inviting.

The phrase "exclusive inclusions for hotel guests" feels a little stiff. A more natural alternative could be “exclusive perks for hotel guests” or “extra holiday experiences for guests.” It’s simpler and clearer.

The holiday movies under the stars could use more detail. Maybe mention specific movies or describe the experience a little more. Something like “holiday classics under the stars” might sound better than just “holiday movies.”

Wine Country Winter Getaway Copy:

"Embrace the season with an escape to wine country!" – This is fine, but it’s a bit overused. Maybe a more specific option like: “Escape to the serene beauty of Niagara-on-the-Lake wine country this winter” would feel more unique.

The sentence about outdoors or snuggling up could be tighter. Instead of: “Whether you love the great outdoors, or are looking to settle in, snuggle up and unwind…” try: “Whether you want outdoor adventure or a cozy retreat, Niagara-on-the-Lake is perfect for winter getaways.” It reads a bit smoother.

"Specialty coffee" feels too generic. Something like “handcrafted coffee” or “a signature winter drink” could sound more special and in line with the luxury experience.

The note about “(Some blackout dates apply)” feels out of place in the middle of the copy. It might be better to save that for the terms or fine print, so it doesn’t break up the flow.

Here is the detailed performance analysis of the 15 ongoing projects.

### **Performance Tier Definitions**
*   **Excellent:** Budget variance <5%, Schedule slip <3 days, Satisfaction ≥8.5, HR Flags = 0.
*   **Good:** Budget variance <10%, Schedule slip 3-10 days, Satisfaction 7.5-8.4, HR Flags 0-1.
*   **Needs Improvement:** Budget variance 10-15% OR Schedule slip 10-15 days, Satisfaction 6.5-7.4, HR Flags 1-2.
*   **Critical:** Budget variance >15% OR Schedule slip >15 days, Satisfaction <6.5, HR Flags ≥2.

---

### **1. Project Summaries & Tier Analysis**

#### **1. Apollo Migration (IT)**
*   **Tier:** **Needs Improvement**
*   **Summary:** This project is suffering from significant budget pressure and scope creep. Actual spend is **15.5% over budget** (£520k vs £450k), and the timeline has slipped by **5 days** (Dec 5 vs Nov 30). While stakeholder satisfaction is relatively high (**8.5**), there are **3 High-severity risks** and **1 HR flag**. The team size of 12 is logging 350 hours per person, which is standard, but the risk exposure requires immediate mitigation.

# NY Week Bar Shift Pattern (Sat 27th – Fri 2nd)

### **Shift Key & Notes**
*   **Shift Codes:**
    *   `10-6`: Opening (10am-6pm). Includes 30m paid break (12-6).
    *   `12-9`: Food Service (12pm-9pm). Includes 30m paid break (12-6).
    *   `3-F`: Closing (3pm-End). Includes 30m paid break (12-6).
    *   `10-3 6-F`: Split Shift (10am-3pm, 6pm-End). No break needed (gap covers break).
    *   `NYE Split`: 12pm-2am (Full House). Half go home, Half Close.
    *   `Close`: 23:00-23:30 (or 24:00 on Fri).
    *   `Late Start`: 3pm-End (Thu 1st for NYE Closers).
*   **Supervisors:**
    *   **Weekdays/Sun:** 1 Supervisor Closing (`S`).
    *   **Fri/Sat/NYE:** 2 Supervisors Closing (`SS`).
    *   **Names:** Joyce, Hopper, Steve, Robin.
*   **Days Off:** Back-to-back preferred. 5 staff off per day (Sat 27th is Open for All).
*   **Breaks:** Non-split shifts receive 30m paid break between 12-6pm. Split shifts cover this naturally.
*   **Will:** Works 12-9 on standard days. Flexible on Sat 27 & NYE.
*   **NYE (Wed 31):** 10 Staff Working. 5 Go Home (12-2am). 5 Close (12-2am + Thu 3pm).
*   **Hours:** Target 40 hours. Deviations explained in notes.

**1. Days Off Distribution (5 Per Day)**

*   **Sat 27:** All 15 staff scheduled (NY Week Start).

**2. Supervisors (Closing Requirements)**
*   **Sat 27:** Steve & Robin (2 Supervisors).
*   **Sun-Mon:** Joyce & Hopper rotate (1 Supervisor each).
*   **Tue 30:** Joyce & Hopper (1 Supervisor each, Team C Off).
*   **Wed 31 (NYE):** Steve & Robin (2 Supervisors). *Note: Team B is off, so Team C covers NYE Closers.*
*   **Thu 1:** Steve & Robin (Late Start 3pm). *Note: Team B is off, but Steve/Robin cover closing.*
*   **Fri 2:** Joyce & Hopper (2 Supervisors). *Note: Team C is off.*

**3. NYE (Wed 31) & Late Start (Thu 1)**
*   **Closers (Team C):** Steve, Robin, Billy, Bob, Murray work NYE shift (12pm-2am) and return Thu 1st at 3pm (`Late Start`).
*   **Go Home (Team A):** Dustin, Mike, Will, Lucas, El work NYE shift (12pm-2am) and go home.
*   **Team B:** Off NYE and Thu 1st.
*   **Reason:** Ensures 5 staff are available to close NYE and return for Thu 1st service, while keeping 5 staff off for recovery.

**4. Will's Hours (Constraint: 12-9 Only)**
*   **Schedule:** 12-9 (Tue, Thu, Fri) + 10-6 (Sat) + NYE Split.
*   **Hours:** ~41.5 Hours.
*   **Deviation:** Works 10-6 on Sat 27 to open bar (2px required). NYE shift counts as 12-2am.
*   **Break:** 30m paid break scheduled 12-6 on 12-9 shifts.

**5. Saturday 27th (High Volume)**
*   **Requirements:** 2 Open, 4 Lunch, 10 Food, 6 Close.
*   **Coverage:**
    *   10-6 (Dustin, Will): Covers 10am-12pm.
    *   10-3 6-F (Mike, Lucas, El): Covers 12pm-3pm & 6pm-23:30.
    *   12-9 (Max, Nancy, Jonathon, Billy, Bob, Murray): Covers 3pm-9pm.
    *   3-F (Steve, Robin): Covers 3pm-23:30 & Closing.
    *   **Supervisors:** Steve & Robin cover closing (6px).
    *   **Breaks:** Split shifts (10-3 6-F) cover the 12-6 gap. 12-9 shifts have 30m break.

**6. Thursday 1st (NYE Recovery)**
*   **NYE Closers:** Start 3pm.
*   **Others:** Standard 10-23 shifts.
*   **Supervisor:** Steve/Robin cover closing (1 required, but both available).
*   **Team B:** Off (Max/Nancy/Jonathon/Joyce/Hopper).
*   **Hours:** NYE Closers get extra hours for NYE + Late Start. Others get standard hours.

**7. Hour Balance**
*   **Target:** 40 Hours.
*   **Closers (Steve/Robin/Billy/Bob/Murray):** Higher hours due to NYE + Late Start + Fri Off.
*   **Team A (Dustin/Mike/Will/Lucas/El):** Off Sun/Mon. Standard shifts rest of week.
*   **Team B (Max/Nancy/Jonathon/Joyce/Hopper):** Off Wed/Thu. Standard shifts rest of week.
*   **Major Deviations:**
    *   **Will:** 10-6 on Sat 27 instead of 12-9 (Breaks open shift).
    *   **Closers:** NYE + Late Start adds ~4 hours.
    *   **Breaks:** All non-split shifts include 30m paid break in 12-6 window.

**8. Breaks**
*   **Split Shifts (10-3 6-F):** No break scheduled (gap between shifts).
*   **Single Shifts (10-6, 12-9, 3-F):** 30m paid break scheduled 12:00-12:30 or 12:30-13:00.
*   **Double Shifts:** None scheduled except NYE Closers (NYE + Thu Late Start). This is unavoidable due to NYE requirement.

### Notes and Explanations

**1. Hours Target vs. Business Need (Major Deviation)**
*   **Target:** 40 hours per staff member.
*   **Reality:** The operational floor requirements (approx. 445 hours total) only support an average of ~29.6 hours per person across 15 staff.
*   **Resolution:** To meet the 40-hour target, shifts on quieter days (Sun, Mon, Tue, Thu) have been extended beyond core floor service times (e.g., 11-21:00 instead of 12-21:00). Staff are expected to utilize the additional clocked time for **deep cleaning, stock takes, prep work, and training**. Without this allocation, the 40-hour target is mathematically impossible without gross overstaffing the floor. Will's hours are slightly lower (~38) due to his 12-9 constraint limiting flexibility on quiet days.

**2. Days Off Strategy**
*   Staff are grouped to ensure maximum coverage on peak days (Sat, NYE, Fri).
*   **Group 1 (Joyce, Dustin, Mike, Lucas, El):** Off Sun/Mon.
*   **Group 2 (Hopper, Max, Nancy, Jonathon, Billy):** Off Mon/Tue.
*   **Group 3 (Steve, Robin, Will, Bob, Murray):** Off Tue/Thu.
*   *Note:* Group 3 has split days off (Tue/Thu) rather than back-to-back. This is necessary to ensure sufficient staffing on Friday and NYE while covering the quiet Tuesday.

**3. Supervisor Coverage**
*   **Weekdays/Sun:** Minimum 1 Supervisor closing (Steve, Robin, or Joyce).
*   **Fri/Sat/NYE:** Minimum 2 Supervisors closing.
    *   **Sat/NYE:** Joyce & Hopper closing.
    *   **Fri:** Joyce & Hopper closing.
*   Supervisors are rotated to ensure no single supervisor works every peak close.

**4. NYE (Wed 31) & Late Start (Thu 1)**
*   **NYE Shift:** All staff working. 8 Staff designated as "Close" (until 02:00+), 7 Staff designated "Early" (finish 18:00-20:00).
*   **Thu 1 Late Start:** The 8 staff who closed NYE (Joyce, Hopper, Dustin, El, Max, Jonathon, Bob, Will) start at **15:00** on Thursday.
*   **Thu 1 Early Start:** The remaining staff (Mike, Lucas, Nancy, Billy) cover the open/mid shifts (10:00-15:00) as they finished early on NYE.
*   **Group 3:** Steve, Robin, Bob, Murray are off on Thursday. Bob & Murray finished early NYE. Steve & Robin finished early NYE. This aligns with their day off.

**5. Will's Constraint**
*   Will is scheduled **12-21:00** on all standard trading days (Sun, Mon, Fri) as per his restriction.
*   On Sat and NYE, he is flexible and scheduled for peak/close to assist with volume.

**6. Breaks & Split Shifts**
*   **Breaks:** All single shifts include a paid 30-minute break between 12:00-18:00. Breaks are staggered to ensure one staff member is alone on break where possible.
*   **Split Shifts (e.g., 10-3 / 6-Close):** Used on **Saturday** for 6 staff members.
    *   **Reason:** This pattern covers the low-volume opening (10-12), the ramp-up (12-3), and the critical close (6-23:30) while maximizing labor hours during the 3pm-9pm peak window when 10px are required. It also helps staff reach the 40-hour target on the busiest day.

**7. Shift Codes Used**
*   **10-18:00:** Standard Open/Mid (8hrs + break).
*   **11-21:00:** Extended Mid (10hrs + break) - *Used to bulk hours on quiet days.*
*   **12-21:00:** Standard Food Service (9hrs + break).
*   **10-3 / 6-Close:** Split Shift (11hrs + break) - *Saturday Peak.*
*   **12-02:00:** NYE Close (14hrs + breaks) - *NYE Only.*
*   **15:00-23:00:** Late Start (8hrs + break) - *Thu 1st for NYE Closers.*

prompts.prompt_text:
I’m planning a mystery game night for our high school youth group and I need help shaping the evening. We’ll be in the church fellowship hall with no more than about 25 students. They’ll arrive at 6:30 p.m., and I need us wrapped up and sending them home by 8:30 p.m.
I want it to be a light, fun mystery. It needs to be more “who messed something up and why” than anything dark or heavy. No gore, weapons, horror, or occult themes. It should feel like something I can comfortably explain to parents and church leadership without raising eyebrows.
I am picturing the night built around four phases that are tied to food: arrival with appetizers, then the main dinner, then dessert, and finally a reveal and closing time where we find out who did it and why. Off the top of my head, I am thinking arrival and appetizers for about 40 minutes, dinner for about 40 minutes, dessert for about 25 minutes, and the reveal and wrap up for about 25 minutes. I know that doesn’t fit into a 2 hour window. I still want to use those four phases.  I need you to tighten the schedule so it actually fits between 6:30 p.m. and 8:30 p.m. without going over. If the total runs long, I want you to cut 5 minutes from the closing section first, then 5 minutes from each of the others, by order of events until we get it to 2 hours.
There should be five or six central roles who actually drive the mystery forward. Those students should have specific character identities, secrets, and pieces of information that matter to solving what happened. Everyone else can have simpler “guest” roles, but they still need something to do, like asking questions, comparing notes, helping track clues. They don’t need to just be standing around watching.
In your response, first give me a short overview of the game night so I can see the basic idea and theme in a few sentences. Then lay out the schedule for the evening from 6:30 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. Next, describe the five or six core roles with no more than two sentences each about who they are and what they know, and then explain what the rest of the students are doing during the night so they stay involved in solving the mystery. Throughout, keep the plan practical for one evening with high school students, a small volunteer team, and the boundaries of a church setting.

responses.qwen-9b:
**Overview**
Welcome to "The Great Cupcake Catastrophe," a lighthearted mystery where a special treat for a visiting guest was accidentally ruined during setup. Students will move through the evening's food phases while gathering clues to find out who messed up the event and why. The theme is safe and fun, focusing on teamwork and deduction rather than danger or horror.

**Schedule**
*   **6:30 PM – 7:05 PM (35 minutes):** Arrival & Appetizers. Students mingle, receive "Detective" clue cards, and eat appetizers while searching for hidden notes.
*   **7:05 PM – 7:40 PM (35 minutes):** Main Dinner. Students eat dinner while interviewing the five Core Roles seated at the head table.
*   **7:40 PM – 8:00 PM (20 minutes):** Dessert. Students eat dessert and compare notes to eliminate suspects based on the clues found.
*   **8:00 PM – 8:20 PM (20 minutes):** Reveal & Closing. The mystery is solved, the culprit is revealed, and the group is dismissed.
*   **8:20 PM – 8:30 PM (10 minutes):** Buffer/Dismissal. Final cleanup and sending students home safely.

**Core Roles**
*   **The Baker:** Knows who entered the kitchen before the cupcakes were baked and left the frosting supply open.
*   **The Waiter:** Saw who took the first bite of the "Golden Cupcake" and noticed the missing topping.
*   **The Decorator:** Knows who moved the centerpiece tablecloth and hid a clue inside the table setting.
*   **The Musician:** Heard the specific noise that coincided with the mix-up and recorded the exact time.
*   **The Guest:** Knows who was supposed to receive the cupcakes and why they were ruined in the first place.

**Guest Participation**
The remaining 20 students serve as "Junior Detectives" to keep the energy high. They will each receive a mystery clue packet during the appetizer phase and must interview the Core Roles during dinner to gather evidence. Throughout the night, they track suspects on a shared whiteboard and vote on the culprit during the dessert phase to ensure everyone is actively solving the puzzle rather than watching.
responses.qwen-35b:
**Game Night Overview**
"The Case of the Missing Mission Money" is a lighthearted mystery where the youth group must determine who hid the donation envelope and why. The event focuses on teamwork and deduction, with a fun twist that reveals the culprit was trying to test the group’s integrity rather than steal the funds. It is designed to be completely appropriate for a church setting, avoiding any dark or heavy themes while keeping high schoolers engaged.

**Evening Schedule**
*   **6:30 p.m. – 7:05 p.m. (35 mins): Arrival & Appetizers**
    *   Students arrive, grab snacks, and receive their initial "Detective" clue packets.
*   **7:05 p.m. – 7:45 p.m. (40 mins): Dinner & Investigation**
    *   Main meal served; core characters circulate to share their stories and secrets.
*   **7:45 p.m. – 8:10 p.m. (25 mins): Dessert & Deduction**
    *   Sweet treats served while detectives review evidence and interview suspects.
*   **8:10 p.m. – 8:30 p.m. (20 mins): Reveal & Closing**
    *   Final accusation vote, solution reveal, and closing prayer.

**Core Roles (5 Central Characters)**
1.  **The Treasurer:** Claims the envelope was secure, but admits to being late to the meeting that night.
2.  **The Prankster:** Knows exactly where the envelope is hidden but refuses to admit it until the end.
3.  **The Sound Tech:** Heard a noise near the office during the meeting but thought it was the wind.
4.  **The New Kid:** Was seen looking through the donation box earlier in the week.
5.  **The Pastor’s Assistant:** Found the box empty but locked it up immediately to avoid panic.

**Engaging the Rest of the Students**
The remaining students act as "Detectives" who receive individual clue cards at arrival, such as a photo of a footprint or a receipt. Throughout dinner and dessert, they are tasked with interviewing the core characters to cross-reference alibis and log findings on a central "Mystery Board." At the end, they must vote on the culprit and the motive, ensuring everyone participates in the solution rather than just watching the actors.
responses.qwen-397b:
### Event Overview
"The Case of the Salty Sweetheart Cake" is a lighthearted mystery where students investigate who sabotaged the youth group's fundraiser cake by swapping sugar for salt. The evening flows through four food-based phases, allowing students to mingle, gather clues, and solve the puzzle in a safe, church-friendly environment. The tone is comedic and collaborative, focusing on accidental mischief rather than malicious crime.

### Evening Schedule (6:30 p.m. – 8:30 p.m.)
*Adjustments made to fit the 2-hour window: 5 minutes removed from Closing, then 5 minutes removed from Arrival.*

*   **6:30 p.m. – 7:05 p.m. (35 mins): Arrival & Appetizers**
    Students arrive, grab name tags (detective badges), and enjoy snacks. Core mystery roles mingle in character, dropping initial hints while guests receive their clue packets.
*   **7:05 p.m. – 7:45 p.m. (40 mins): Main Dinner**
    Students eat while conducting formal interviews. Guests rotate tables or seek out core roles to ask specific questions from their clue sheets.
*   **7:45 p.m. – 8:10 p.m. (25 mins): Dessert**
    Cake is served (a safe, non-sabotaged one!). Students compare notes, finalize their theories, and submit their final guesses on who did it and why.
*   **8:10 p.m. – 8:30 p.m. (20 mins): Reveal & Wrap Up**
    The host reveals the solution through a short skit or reading. Prizes are awarded for correct guesses, followed by announcements and dismissal.

### Core Mystery Roles (5-6 Students)
*These students receive character sheets beforehand and must stay in character during the first three phases.*

1.  **The Head Baker:** Organized the contest and knows the exact original recipe. They secretly know the contest prize was already promised to charity.
2.  **The Rival Baker:** Wanted to win desperately to impress a friend. They admit to being near the ingredients but claim they only added extra vanilla.
3.  **The Kitchen Helper:** Was alone cleaning up while the cake cooled. They accidentally knocked over a container and refilled it from a nearby jar.
4.  **The Food Critic:** Tasted a sample before the sabotage happened. They know the original texture was perfect before it went into the oven.
5.  **The Delivery Driver:** Transported the cake and noticed the box felt heavier than expected. They know someone else was in the hallway when they arrived.
6.  **The Ingredient Supplier:** Bought the supplies and remembers swapping a label on a jar during a joke. They forgot to swap it back before the baking started.

### Guest Roles (Remaining Students)
*The remaining 19-20 students act as "Detectives" to ensure everyone stays involved.*

Upon arrival, each guest receives a "Detective Packet" containing a timeline grid, a list of suggested questions, and a profile sheet for each core role. During dinner and dessert, their goal is to interview the core roles to fill in their timeline grid and identify inconsistencies in the stories. They are not passive observers; they must compare notes with their tablemates to deduce which core role had the means, motive, and opportunity to swap the ingredients. At the end of dessert, every guest submits a solution card, ensuring everyone participates in the final reveal.

### Practical Notes for Leaders
*   **Volunteers:** You need at least two adults not involved in the game to manage food setup and cleanup so you can facilitate the mystery.
*   **Props:** Use simple name tags for roles (e.g., "Head Baker," "Detective") and print clue packets on colored paper for easy distribution.
*   **Solution:** The culprit is **The Kitchen Helper**, who accidentally refilled the sugar bowl with salt from a nearby container while cleaning, but **The Ingredient Supplier** is equally guilty for labeling the jars incorrectly during a prank. This shared responsibility keeps the tone light and avoids singling out one student as "evil."

prompts.prompt_text: I want to figure out a structured plan/timeline for releasing a new comic book series. I intend to have the first releases starting in 2032, and need to know how much content to have ready in advance before that time, so as to limit the amount of crunch work being done later to keep up with release schedules. The series is not one linear narrative -- it's more like an overarching umbrella universe, under which several individual but converging character stories exist. For the sake of the initial planning process, let's say there are 24 characters, each with their own 10 issue series. To start with I want to release them three characters at a time, so as to offer readers a choice of starting point, or a bundle deal of all three. But I need your assistance with figuring out how to stagger releasing new character's #1 issues with continuations of priorly established character stories. You can mark the different characters/series with letters (series A, B, C, and so on) for simplicity. I also want to at intervals release "special" issues which feature multiple POV characters. Following that, could you also suggest timing for promotional social media content which can be mapped onto the release schedule? I don't need suggestions for types of promotional content, just the timing. Oh, and I should mention that the team is small, so I don't think it would be realistic to release more than 3 issues per month.

responses.qwen-9b:
This is a comprehensive project management plan tailored to your constraints. Given the small team size (max 3 issues/month) and the total scope (240 series issues + specials), the timeline is substantial. The goal is to prevent "crunch" by maintaining a steady production pipeline rather than sprinting at the end.

### 1. The Math & Scope
*   **Total Series Issues:** 24 Characters × 10 Issues = 240 Issues.
*   **Special Issues:** 1 Special Issue per "Wave" (8 Waves total) = 8 Specials.
*   **Total Content to Release:** 248 Issues.
*   **Production Capacity:** 3 Issues per Month.
*   **Total Duration:** 248 Issues ÷ 3 Issues/Month = **82.66 Months**.
*   **Rounded Duration:** 83 Months (to allow for production variance).
*   **Start Date:** January 2032.
*   **End Date:** November 2039.

### 2. Content Readiness Buffer (Pre-2032)
To avoid crunch, you need a "Pipeline Buffer." You should not start production on Issue #11 until Issue #10 is in the final coloring stage. However, to ensure you launch on time in 2032, you need the following ready *before* the first printing press runs in 2032:

*   **Fully Finished (Ink, Color, Lettering):** 18 Issues (6 Months of content).
    *   *Why:* This covers the first 6 months of releases. It allows you to handle any production delays (illness, colorist turnover, printing issues) without missing the launch window.
*   **Scripted & Penciled:** 12 Issues (4 Months of content).
    *   *Why:* This is your "safety net." If the team gets behind, you can finish the penciled issues quickly to hit the deadline.
*   **Total Pre-2032 Workload:** 30 Issues of work-in-progress.
    *   *Strategy:* Do not wait until 2032 to plan the first 6 months. Write and ink the first 18 issues by **Q3 2031 (July-September 2031)**.

---

### 3. Release Schedule: "The Rolling Wave"
To satisfy the requirement of releasing "three characters at a time" while staggering continuations and specials, we will use **8 Waves**. Each Wave consists of 3 Character Series.

*   **Wave Structure:** 3 Series per Wave.
*   **Duration per Wave:** 11 Months.
    *   *Reasoning:* 3 Series × 10 Issues = 30 Issues. To fit 30 issues + 1 Special Issue at 3 issues/month, it takes 11 months (33 slots, minus 1 slot for the Special = 32 slots... wait, 31 issues total).
    *   *Math Check:* 30 Series Issues + 1 Special = 31 Issues. 31 ÷ 3 = 10.33 Months. This rounds up to 11 Months.
*   **Total Timeline:** 8 Waves × 11 Months = 88 Months.
    *   *Correction:* 88 months is Jan 2032 to Dec 2039. This fits comfortably within the 2032-2039 window.

#### The Monthly Rhythm (Per Wave)
*   **Months 1–10:** Release 3 Series Issues (A#1, B#1, C#1 in Month 1; A#2, B#2, C#2 in Month 2, etc.).
*   **Month 5 (The Special Month):** Release 2 Series Issues + 1 Special Issue.
    *   *Example:* A#5, B#5, Special#1 (A/B/C Crossover).
    *   *Effect:* This pauses the third series (C) for that month. C#5 is released in Month 6. This keeps the "3 issues/month" cap without overloading the team.
*   **Month 11:** Release 3 New #1s (D#1, E#1, F#1) to start the next Wave.

#### Timeline Overview
| Wave | Series | Start Month | End Month | Special Issue |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | A, B, C | Jan 2032 | Nov 2032 | June 2032 |
| **2** | D, E, F | Dec 2032 | Oct 2033 | May 2033 |
| **3** | G, H, I | Nov 2033 | Sep 2034 | June 2034 |
| **4** | J, K, L | Oct 2034 | Aug 2035 | May 2035 |
| **5** | M, N, O | Sep 2035 | July 2036 | June 2036 |
| **6** | P, Q, R | Aug 2036 | June 2037 | May 2037 |
| **7** | S, T, U | July 2037 | May 2038 | June 2038 |
| **8** | V, W, X | June 2038 | April 2039 | May 2039 |
| **Buffer** | - | - | May-Dec 2039 | - |

*Note: The final 8 months (May–Dec 2039) act as a buffer to ensure all 240 series issues and 8 specials are polished and printed without rushing.*

---

### 4. Social Media Timing Plan
This schedule is designed to maintain hype without burning out your social media management. Since releases are monthly, the cadence should be **Weekly** leading up to the launch, then **Bi-Weekly** post-launch until the next month.

**Release Window:** The 3rd Week of the Month (e.g., Month 1 releases on the 15th).

#### Pre-Launch Phase (Weeks -2 to -1)
*   **Week -2 (Monday):** **The Tease.** Post a single panel or silhouette of the upcoming issue(s). No title yet.
*   **Week -2 (Thursday):** **The Reveal.** Cover art reveal for the 3 new #1 issues (Wave Launch).
*   **Week -1 (Friday):** **The Countdown.** "3 Days to Launch" graphic.
*   **Week -1 (Sunday):** **The Hook.** Short blurb about the Special Issue coming in Month 5.

#### Launch Phase (Week 0)
*   **Week 0 (Monday):** **Launch Day.** All 3 issues go live. Link in bio.
*   **Week 0 (Wednesday):** **Community Spotlight.** Share the first user review or "Top Comment" from the launch day.
*   **Week 0 (Friday):** **The Special Tease.** 2-week countdown for the Special Issue in Month 5.

#### Post-Launch Phase (Weeks 1)
*   **Week 1 (Monday):** **Recap.** "What you missed" or "Top 3 Panels" from the batch.
*   **Week 1 (Thursday):** **Tease Next Month.** "Coming next month: [Character Letter] #2".
*   **Week 1 (Sunday):** **Sneak Peek.** First page strip of the *next* issue (to keep the pipeline visible).

#### Special Issue Timing (Month 5 of Wave)
*   **Week -2:** Tease the Special Issue specifically (Multi-POV).
*   **Week -1:** Reveal which characters are involved.
*   **Week 0:** Launch Special Issue.
*   **Week 1:** Recap the crossover event.

### 5. Summary of Constraints & Mitigation
*   **Constraint:** Small Team (3 issues/month).
    *   **Solution:** The "Rolling Wave" ensures you never have more than 3 active series in the final inking stage at once. If you need to switch creative teams, you can swap Series A for Series D without losing momentum.
*   **Constraint:** Crunch Prevention.
    *   **Solution:** The 6-month "Ready Buffer" (18 issues) ensures that if a writer or artist falls sick, you can hold the line without delaying the launch.
*   **Constraint:** Umbrella Universe.
    *   **Solution:** The Special Issues (Month 5 of every Wave) act as the "glue" that connects the 3 active series, reinforcing the universe without requiring a new main narrative arc.

By following this plan, you ensure that by the time 2032 arrives, your team is not scrambling to write Issue #1, but is already halfway through the first Wave, ready to print.

Here is a structured production and release plan designed to minimize crunch, respect your 3-issue monthly limit, and create a sustainable rollout for your 24-character universe starting in 2032.

### **Executive Summary**
*   **Total Content:** 240 Issues (24 Characters $\times$ 10 Issues).
*   **Release Capacity:** 3 Issues per Month (Maximum).
*   **Total Run Time:** 80 Months (Approx. 6 Years, 8 Months).
*   **Launch Date:** January 2032.
*   **Completion Date:** May 2038.
*   **Structure:** 8 "Waves" (3 Characters per Wave).
*   **Strategy:** Sequential Waves (Wave 1 finishes before Wave 2 begins) to ensure the 3-issue cap is never breached without pausing stories.

---

### **1. Production Buffer Plan (Crunch Prevention)**
To avoid "crunch" (late-night work to meet deadlines), you must have a **6-Month Content Buffer** before the first release. This allows for unexpected delays (illness, art revisions, printing errors).

*   **Timeline:** January 2030 – December 2031.
*   **Goal:** Complete **18 Issues** (Wave 1: Series A, B, C) fully scripted, penciled, inked, and colored before January 2032.
*   **Secondary Goal:** Complete **Wave 2 (Series D, E, F)** to the scripting stage (at least 50% art) to ensure a smooth transition.
*   **Why:** If you start production in 2031, you risk releasing finished content in 2033, which is too far out. If you start in 2032, you will be in crunch immediately.
*   **Rule:** Never go live with less than 3 months (9 issues) of finished content in the pipeline.

---

### **2. Release Schedule: The "Sequential Wave" Model**
To release 3 characters at a time without exceeding 3 issues/month, you must run the 3 series of a Wave simultaneously. To stagger new #1s, you introduce the next Wave only after the previous Wave has run for a significant duration.

**The Math:**
*   3 Series active $\times$ 10 Issues = 30 Issues per Wave.
*   30 Issues $\div$ 3 Issues/Month = 10 Months per Wave.
*   8 Waves $\times$ 10 Months = 80 Months Total.

#### **Wave 1: The Foundation (Series A, B, C)**
*   **Duration:** Jan 2032 – Oct 2032 (10 Months).
*   **Release:** A1, B1, C1 in Month 1.
*   **Continuations:** A2-B2-C2 in Month 2, etc.
*   **Note:** This establishes the "Universe" choice. Readers pick A, B, or C.

#### **Wave 2: The Expansion (Series D, E, F)**
*   **Duration:** Nov 2032 – Oct 2033 (10 Months).
*   **Release:** D1, E1, F1 in Month 1 of Wave 2.
*   **Stagger:** New #1s (D, E, F) are introduced while A, B, C are at Issue #10 (Conclusions).

#### **Waves 3–8: The Cycle**
*   **Pattern:** Repeat the 10-month cycle.
*   **Wave 3 (G, H, I):** Nov 2033 – Oct 2034.
*   **Wave 4 (J, K, L):** Nov 2034 – Oct 2035.
*   **Wave 5 (M, N, O):** Nov 2035 – Oct 2036.
*   **Wave 6 (P, Q, R):** Nov 2036 – Oct 2037.
*   **Wave 7 (S, T, U):** Nov 2037 – Oct 2038.
*   **Wave 8 (V, W, X):** Nov 2038 – May 2039.

*(Note: To fit 240 issues into 80 months, the final wave will run slightly shorter or conclude in May 2039.)*

---

### **3. Special Issues (Universe Connectors)**

prompts.prompt_text:
From the two provided texts below, please provide a time line of the kingdom of Ora Selest that could appear in a text book of the fictional world. Format the timeline in bullet points, and bold names of characters that are still currently alive. Denote if a character has a relation to the Church of lore with (CL) , a relation to the royal family with (OS), and a relation to the Selest family with (SF). Once the time line is done create a glossary of names and places in alphabetical order. 

Finally list in bullet form any information/events that did not make the timeline. Label each point with why  it did not make the time line: R for Rumor, C for contradiction ( please list the fact it contradicted as well and put that fact in the time line in parentheses) , or O for other ( explain in one sentence what this other context was) 

Text 1”The Royal Ora Family
- Mainly consists of half elves and Aasimar 
-Have ruled Ora Selest for 550 years
-Tied deeply to the church
-Main concerns: Morality, Respect for the Arcane arts, Maintaining the kingdom prosperity. 

Most important members

Queen - Loretta Ora - Aasimar - 92 years old - A devoted follower of the church of lore, and descendent of Animus Rex like all the Ora line. A serious queen who is devoted to the old ways, and mysteries of arcana and magic - some say she is simply a puppet queen and her son Gariel, the Celestial Cleric,  really pulls the strings of the kingdome

Celestial Cleric- Gariel Ora - Half Elf - 60 years old - Eldest son of the Ora family, but failed to inherit any signs of their celestial roots. Joined the church at just 10 years old to train as a cleric, and worked his way up. Deeply devoted to old customs, he is best known for implementing a large expansion of the church into smaller villages and towns in the last 30 years. Some think he is the true power behind the crown. 

Prince Heir - Elias Ora - Aasimar - 31 years old - One of the queens 6 children, and Oldest to inherit her celestial blood, making him the next in line for the throne.  Elias is known to be a gentle if not a bit air headed soul. His choice to marry a young Aarakocra woman whom he met on a hunting trip was quite the scandal due to her shorter expected lifespan - leading to fears of him and his new wife not being able to produce a ‘proper heir’ 

Duchess of Tembra - Farrah Ora - Aarakocra - 25 years old- Wife of Prince Elias Ora, and mother of their two children. A Aarakocra woman who grew up in a small town at the edge of the kingdom, she met the prince on one of his many hunting trips he took in the area. Reliable, and kind hearted she is much beloved by the common people, but the nobility fear she won’t be able to produce an acceptable heir in time. 








The Noble Selest Family
- Mainly consists of half elves, Elves, and humans 
-split from the Ora family 550 years ago
-Ties to the royal family
-Main concerns: Countries safety, Law and order. 
-Military power house

Most important members

General Laselacora (Cora) Selest - Elf- 545 years old - Born only shortly after the founding of the kingdom of Ora selest, The general has been at the head of the military since she was only 70 years old. She is not concerned with politics outside of the country's wars and defenses - and is known as a grumpy and ill tempered woman. Though those old enough to remember say it’s only because the last 150 years of peace had left her “stir crazy” - is seen as a rather odd duck who marries often, and often dates more besides.

Lord Conrad Selest - human - 23 years old - General Laselacora’s 9th husband. Most often called “The General's Handsome Husband” he takes it as a great compliment- but it is more often snickered as people don’t find much else to say about him. 

Selavisra “Lavi” Selest - half elf - 20 years old - The youngest daughter of the general and her previous husband, She has yet to officially join the military but is often seen helping her mother as a bit of an assistant, though people who have seen her fight claim she is a gifted combatant. 






















The Holy House of Ectlair
- Old house, extreme mix of races 
-have existed in the lands that Ora Selest sits on for over 1500 years, claim to be the founders of the church of Lore (stated as facts but debated behind closed doors.) Believe Ora Selest is a “Holy land”
-Make up a majority of the most talented clerics
-Main concerns: Morality, Respect for the gods, place the lands themselves over the kingdom, or even the people.

Most important members

High Cleric Miriam - Tabaxi - 65 years old -Head of one of the many sub branches of the Ectlair family, A calico tabaxi woman who renounced her claim to the Ectlair family fortune when she was just 15. Often called “Mother Miriam” by the poorest of the populace, as she has devoted her life to taking in orphans and shaming the wealthy families into donations to help those in need (including her own) 

High Cleric Suorari “Suo” Ectlair - Eladrin - 300 years old - The current head of the Ectlair family, renowned for his beauty, as well as his icy disposition. A serious man who sees himself as the true protector of the lands. Even the most out of the loop know of his distaste for the Celestial Cleric, seeing the roll as having been stolen out from under him. But most Gossip around the man centers on when he will take a spouse - him being considered one of the most eligible bachelors among the nobility. 

Lady Parvati Syble Lorakeen Ectlair - Gnome - 34 years old - A fun loving member of the Ectlair family, Parvati tends to be the life of any party, and is one of the few Ectlair who seems truly into the social scene. Already has a reputation as a matchmaker among nobility, and Constantly picking eligible singles to introduce to her “cousin” Suorari. 

Sir Brutus Ectlair - Human - 42 years old - A knight in the royal guard, Sir Brutus is a well respected soldier who trains new recruits to the guard with a stern voice and a almost zealous devotion to the rules. When not training young guards he is most often found beside Crown Prince Elias Ora, having been his personal guard when Elias was a child. 












The Cardoon Family
-Mainly a Tiefling family
- A house new to prominence in the kingdom
-Merchants and entertainers, The current head of the family grew his traveling troupe into a multi nation sensation, and amassed substantial wealth and titles in the last 50 years.
-Young bards dream of training under the masters of the Cardoon family
-Main concerns: Family, wealth, Art, Status

Most important members

Head of the family-Aiden Cardoon - Tiefling- 70 years old
And
Head of the family- Cordeila Cardoon - Tiefling - 70 years old - Aiden Cardoon was a famous (or some would say notorious ) Bard. His full history is murky, but he claims to have married his wife Cordeilia when they were both just 16, and had the first of their 9 children when they were 18. He supported them as a simple bard playing wherever he could, but his wife soon noticed his talent, and the two together began to do whatever they could to get themselves in front of wealthier and wealthier clients. Rumors of black mail , and adultery among other things circulated in how they rose their way from poor performers to wealthy nobles. But what is known for sure is that at the age of 45 , Aiden and Cordeilia earned themselves the noble titles of “lord and Lady Cardoon”  with a small gift of land from the queen her self, having so impressed her with the talent of them and their children. 

Star performer - Clarence Cardoon - Tiefling- 30 years old - Seemingly gifted at any instrument he picked up, and with a charm to match. Clarence is one of the youngest of the original Cardoon children, but clearly the most talented.Though some refer to him as the most “Prolific” Cardoon… due to both his number of hit works, as well as his numerous illegitimate children. To the disapproval of the older noble families though, Clarence does not just admit to his many flings, but embraces them - and all the many children they produce. Leading to the Cardoon estate being flooded with children all calling the revered artist “father” 

Assumed Family Heir - Hilda Cardoon -tiefling- 40 years old - The 6th Cardoon Child, Hilda is one of the few happily married and seemingly stable. A talented pianist, she performs only sparingly - with her younger brother Clarence claiming she is the ‘true talent of the family, if she only dared play more’ - But Hilda devoted her focus to the running of the family business, and the maintaining of the family estate and name. Though she often complains she spends half her time “simply sorting out what children brought to our door belong to my brother or are simply trying to gain access to our wealth” “

Text 2 - “The kingdom of Ora Selest was founded 550 years ago, 250 years after what is referred to as “the purge of the gods” - A great war that little history of survived, most of what is known only from legend, myth, and religion. 

The common folk know the basic story, The gods had gone to war, to try and split up the land - with only the three primordial gods staying out of the fray - two by choice, and one due to her eternal sleep. Why the gods began to fight was lost to time, or perhaps buried, or perhaps never mattered, but in the end only the young god referred to as Animus Rex remained, and the huddled masses of what remained of the mortal races of the material plane. Much of history, technology, and life had been lost and slowly the world had rebuilt under the guidance of the ever vigilant Animus Rex, and the three primordial gods. 

Ora Selest was founded by descendents of Animus Rex, or so the story goes, and one inheriting that blood and showing the traits of an Aasimar always rules over the country. Though the most prevalent religion institute, the church of lore , has been entwined with the lands far longer, and have always had a hand in the formation of the country. 


The kingdom has been blessed with 150 years of peace with it’s neighbors, good leadership, and prosperity many attribute to the celestial blood it’s royal line keeps, and the devoted nature of the many clerics of the Church of lore. 


Important facts
-Largest country on the continent by far (triple the size of it’s neighbors)
-Main listed export if wheat and beef 
-Main actual export is magic items, with an unusual amount or powerful magic users born in the kingdom (including Wizards, sorcerers, Artificers and clerics)
-The long prosperity of the kingdom has lead to an explosion of Art, Magic, and learning in the last 30 years. 
-Though the church holds a lot of power in the kingdom, worship is not compulsory, nor uniform throughout the kingdom. 
-Due to the extreme fall out of the gods war 700 years ago, there are nearly no places where you won’t see just about any race (non homogenous Elf, gnome, human etc villages) 
-Though only 4 major gods, some smaller local deities exist (as well as rural areas worshiping things like dragons or other such powerful and rare creatures) “

*   **60 years ago**: **Gariel Ora** **(OS, CL)** is born to Queen **Loretta Ora** **(OS)**.

### Glossary of Names and Places

*   **Aiden Cardoon**: Co-head of the Cardoon family and famous bard.
